blocks.label: School Experience
blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan is currently a ninth grade student enrolled at Ridgeway High School, under the RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA Special Education Local Plan Area (SELPA). She attends through a virtual meeting format and has previously been enrolled by her parents in a private school and Options for Youth Home School. Emma Rose began formal schooling in a Chinese/English bilingual preschool setting, including Sunshine Bilingual Preschool and Bright Start Preschool, prior to entering elementary school. During her elementary years, Emma Rose attended Oak Meadow School and Creekside Oaks and was first assessed for special education services in fourth grade (Fairhaven initial IEP).

Emma Rose has consistently demonstrated academic strengths in basic reading, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, and spelling. Early assessments highlight relative strengths, such as oral reading fluency and essay composition, while math problem solving and written expression emerged as areas of need. Oral reading fluency scores were strong, with Emma Rose reading grade level text at 52 correct words per minute (CWPM) and showing accuracy gains through elementary years. She is currently reading at a seventh-grade level based on her edmentum diagnostic, and her recent diagnostic score (989) places her at the 18th national percentile. Vocabulary development and comprehension have also been noted, with a recent vocabulary quiz score of 15/25 and performance in reading literature and informational text near basic proficiency.

Math fluency and numerical operations remain significant challenges. Current school reports describe ongoing areas of academic weakness in math fluency and numerical operations, supported by subtest scores in Algebra & Expressions (3/11), Fractions & Ratios (3/11), Geometry (3/10), Measurement, Data & Statistics (1/11), and Numbers & Operations (5/11). Emma Rose’s proficiency in addition, subtraction, and multiplication within 100 is relatively strong, though multi-step word problems and higher-level math reasoning tasks are inconsistent. The need for continued support in math reasoning is reflected in goal statements, and Emma Rose’s recent summative assessment indicates improvement with an 86% accuracy score.

Written expression has been a persistent area of difficulty. Emma Rose can write expository essays with emerging topic sentences and supporting details with moderate accuracy (approximately 75%). She expresses creativity in her writing, utilizing metaphors and engaging in reflective essay topics. Despite growth, she formulates responses with frequent errors in grammar, punctuation, and sentence structure, which are targeted in her IEP goals. Emma Rose’s teachers note that she is capable of summarizing articles for health and physical education and shows potential in public speaking. School staff report good attendance, ability to follow directions, and evidence of self-confidence, though she reports a personal dislike for math.

Emma Rose is currently participating in SAI English and Study Skills courses, and areas of need continue to focus on math fluency, written expression, and transition planning.

blocks.label: Intervention
blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan’s intervention history has included a range of supports tailored to her academic and social-emotional needs. Currently, she receives Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in Study Skills for 258 minutes each week, in addition to monthly college and career awareness services (15 minutes each). SAI support is provided in both the general education setting (with accommodations) and in a pull-out format through the Resource Specialist Program (RSP). Specialized Academic Instruction is also targeted toward math, reflecting her ongoing challenges with math fluency and reasoning.

Emma Rose’s intervention plan includes support in study skills and transition. Early intervention during fourth grade included short-term counseling with the school psychologist for self-regulation, coping strategies, and transition support—meeting twice monthly for 30 minutes from May to November 2019. Current goals continue to focus on improving math fluency, written expression, and transition skills as measured by classwork and teacher records.

blocks.label: IEP / Special Education
blocks.prose:
An Individualized Education Program (IEP) is currently in place for Emma Rose Callahan, with a primary eligibility of Specific Learning Disability (SLD). Her IEP outlines areas of need, including math fluency, written expression, and transition skills. No 504 plan is noted as being in place. Emma’s initial IEP was developed during her fourth grade year, and she has continued to receive special education services since that time, including resource support and Specialized Academic Instruction.

IEP meetings are scheduled regularly to review her progress and update her goals. Accommodations and services described in her plan, such as SAI English, study skills, and targeted math support, are provided to address her specific learning needs and to help her access the general education curriculum.

Develop each labeled block in the form demonstrated by the provided example. A block may use one paragraph, several connected paragraphs, a table position, or structured interview responses when the section calls for them. Use the supplied evidence to select concrete details, organize events clearly over time, and preserve who reported second-hand information. Let the amount and shape of the evidence determine the block's depth.

The section should read as one part of a coherent report: factual, specific, accessible to families, and natural rather than formulaic.

Return the requested section content in the supplied output format.

**SCHOOL HISTORY**

Complete cumulative school records were viewed by this evaluator and are summarized as follows:

Diego Fenton was a student in the Fairview City School District from  kindergarten through 8th grades where he attended Green Oaks Elementary and Hartwell Middle School. Attendance was consistently good. In kindergarten and first grades he was noted to need to work on handwriting but met all other expectations. Diego Fenton received additional small group writing instruction for handwriting (letter formation and spacing) in first grade and for punctuation and handwriting in second grade. Behaviorally, Diego Fenton was noted to be socially enthusiastic about learning, but needed improvement in staying on task, following rules and focusing on precision and accuracy. He was at grade level in all areas except writing, which was slightly below. Diego Fenton met standards in third grade but continued to demonstrate attention difficulties. In fourth grade during the first trimester, in Language Arts, Diego Fenton was noted to “exhibit poor listening skills by engaging in side conversations.” There were no other concerns noted through fifth grades and all areas socially, behaviorally, and academically were rated at the proficient or basic levels.

The COVID-19 Pandemic caused schools to move to distance learning during the third semester of seventh grade. Prior to lock-down, during the first two semesters, Diego Fenton did well meeting standards in World Languages, Physical Education, Speaking and Listening and Reading, but he was below grade level expectations in all other areas. Learning behaviors including work completion and utilizing feedback and resources were problematic in Language Arts and Social Studies, but more consistent in all other classes. During Distance Learning, the Physical Education teacher noted that “Interventions were provided, including sit administrator and psychologist/counselor, but the student rarely participated in DL.” Diego Fenton passed all of his classes in 8th grade but demonstrated inconsistent work completion and engagement.

Diego Fenton holds a 1.41 total GPA at Meadowbrook High School where he enrolled in August 2021 as a freshman. Diego Fenton has attempted 155 credits and passed 125. He needs 135 more credits to graduate. Diego Fenton did well his first semester of freshman year, earning a 2.75 grade point average. By second semester, his GPA went down to 1.50 and included significant discipline infractions included fighting, being out of class without permission, walking around in the wetlands behind campus during school, and being disrespectful towards staff. Diego Fenton reported this was when he began using drugs and alcohol. Last year as a sophomore, Diego Fenton had a total of seven absences, 39 periods tardy, 34 period truancies and ten days suspension. Suspensions were due to profanity, possession of drug paraphernalia/ vaping products, and possession of a controlled substance on school grounds.  This semester grades at first progress check were Positive Power- A, Weight Conditioning- A+, CCIM1- B and  US History- C with the comment, “Showing Improvement.”

The report completed by Meadowbrook High School indicated that In September of 2022, Diego Fenton was diagnosed as having Bi-Polar Disorder with Psychosis, ADHD-Combined Type, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder by Family Nurse Practitioner, Tanya Brooks, before she knew he was abusing drugs. In October 2022, Dr. Manning diagnosed Diego Fenton with Opioid Use Disorder, due to an addiction to Fentanyl. Adriana Fenton reportedly requested a 504 meeting to address the diagnoses and the possibility of implementing a Behavior Intervention Plan. After Diego Fenton was again suspended due to possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia/vaping products, parents signed an assessment plan. A 504 Accommodation plan for these diagnoses was put in place in December 2022 with the following accommodations:

1.     Diego Fenton is allowed to take a maximum of one short break per period to the wellness center when showing signs of inattention or frustration. Usually seen by bouncing his leg or being very fidgety. Student will use a card on his desk as a non-verbal que that he needs a break.

2.     Preferential seating near teacher’s primary area of instruction.

3.     Non-verbal and/or subtle redirection when off-task.

During student observations in two classes by the examiner, the above listed accommodations were implemented, with the exception of #1, which was not needed.
